title: LONGER RAY5 Mini and Nano Pro: Small Lasers Compared
metaDescription: LONGER's two compact laser families compared: the RAY5 Mini 2.5W and 3.5W (from $99.32) against the portable Nano 6W and Nano Pro 12W, with area, precision and stated wood cutting.
author: ByteBuy Team

sections.content: Small laser engravers solve two different problems. The RAY5 Mini is a low-cost desktop machine for small projects, from $99.32. The Nano and Nano Pro are portable machines with two diode lasers and much higher prices, from $499 to $594.86. Both families have a small work area, 130x140 mm for the Mini and 100x100 mm for the Nano, so the choice is not about size but about power, precision and what you will engrave.

items.label: RAY5 Mini 2.5W ($99.32)
items.value: 130x140 mm, 0.04 mm precision, 12,000 mm/min, listed for wood, acrylic and leather

items.label: RAY5 Mini 3.5W ($110.35)
items.value: Same size and precision, 3.5W, listed for wood, acrylic, leather and metal

items.label: Nano 6W ($499)
items.value: 100x100 mm, 0.05 mm precision, two diode lasers with FAC, stated 6 mm wood cut, LightBurn and LaserGRBL

items.label: Nano Pro 12W ($594.86)
items.value: 100x100 mm, 0.02 mm precision with field lens, two diode lasers with FAC, stated 10 mm wood cut

pros: The RAY5 Mini 2.5W costs $99.32, the lowest price of any laser in our catalog, with a finer 0.04 mm precision than the larger RAY5
The 3.5W Mini adds metal to the listed materials for only $11 more
The Nano Pro lists 0.02 mm precision with a field lens, the finest figure in the LONGER range
The Nano and Nano Pro list stated wood cutting of 6 mm and 10 mm, so they are the only models here that claim cutting
Both Nano models work with LightBurn and LaserGRBL, popular desktop laser programs
cons: The Mini's 130x140 mm area is small, and the Nano's 100x100 mm area is smaller, so neither suits large projects
The Nano costs about five times the Mini, and the Nano Pro about six times, so you pay a lot for portability and power
The 2.5W Mini is listed for wood, acrylic and leather, so check the listing before assuming it can mark metal
The same models appear several times at different prices, for example the 3.5W Mini at $110.35 and $119.99, so compare listings
Stated cutting depths are best cases and depend on material and passes

items.question: Which one should I buy first?
items.answer: For small engraving projects such as keychains, tags and leather marks, the RAY5 Mini is the sensible start. Choose the Nano Pro only if you need portability and finer detail and are ready to pay for it.

items.question: 2.5W or 3.5W Mini?
items.answer: The 3.5W costs about $11 more and its listing mentions metal as a material, while the 2.5W listing mentions wood, acrylic and leather. Another 2.5W listing at $129 also mentions metal, so read the title of the exact listing you open.

items.question: What is the difference between the Nano and Nano Pro?
items.answer: The Pro lists 12W against 6W, 0.02 mm precision against 0.05 mm, a field lens and a 10 mm wood cut against 6 mm. It costs about $96 more in our listings.

items.question: Can these cut thick wood?
items.answer: Not in a meaningful way. The Nano models list 6 mm and 10 mm wood cutting. For thicker material, look at larger machines such as the LONGER RAY5 20W or B1.

items.question: Are lasers this small safe?
items.answer: A small machine can still burn eyes and skin. Use laser-rated eye protection, ventilate the room and do not leave it running unattended.

sections.content: If you want to engrave small things cheaply, buy a RAY5 Mini, and take the 3.5W if you need to mark metal. If you need a portable machine with some cutting ability and fine detail, the Nano is the entry model and the Nano Pro is the precision option. Check the exact listing, because the same models appear at several prices.
